operations.name: Craig Simpson

expected.name: Craig Simpson
expected.description: Craig Simpson was a pacifist organizer with War Resisters League Southwest in Albuquerque. Beginning in the early 1970s, he organized resistance at Kirtland Air Force Base, Sandia and Los Alamos laboratories, supported GI resistance, and helped create the New Mexico Peace Conversion Project and Cactus Alliance. On September 7, 1981, Simpson joined the Coalition for Direct Action at WIPP protest near Carlsbad. He pleaded no contest to trespass, refused to pay a $50 fine, and served seven days in jail before paying the remaining balance and returning to work.
expected.body:
WIPP custody documented by participant

Dorie Bunting reports the September 7, 1981 demonstrators were taken to Eddy County Jail overnight. Tuesday September 8 arraignment is followed by Simpson receiving two days and a $50 fine; refusal to pay resulted in a ten-day term. The actual release day remains unverified. The existing reported seven days served is retained, not converted into a calculated release date.

Source: Dorie Bunting, WRL News, November-December 1981, printed page 3. Entire original page visually checked. The uncaptioned march faces were not assigned to individual profiles.

operations.name: Paul Emerson Hood

expected.name: Paul Emerson Hood
expected.description: Paul Emerson Hood was a Quaker peace activist and co-founder of Ailanthus, a Boston-area Christian nonviolence community. After serving as a Marine in World War II, he devoted much of his later life to peace work. Ailanthus maintained weekly vigils at Draper Laboratory in Cambridge, where guidance systems for nuclear missiles were developed. Hood was arrested after an August 6, 1981 prayer protest in the laboratory courtyard, received a 30-day sentence, and was released September 25. He later co-founded the Vermont peace group Chrysalis and helped establish the Small Potatoes meal program in Burlington.
expected.body:
Separate 1981 actions and custody limits

The original October 30, 1981 Nuclear Resister, printed page 3, visually inspected, individually names Paul Hood, Jean Holladay and Grace Carson, gives the August 6 arrest and September 25 prison release, and reports thirty-day sentences. It does not give an actual admission date or certify thirty days actually served.

The complete original Commonwealth v. Hood, 389 Mass. 581, including its companion-case footnote, describes a different December 21, 1981 leafleting arrest involving Paul Hood, Suzanne Belote, Robert W. Hillegass and Jean Holladay. The opinion reports $50 fines suspended pending appeal and affirms the convictions July 5, 1983. Neither this decision date nor the later Quaker memorial biography's undated account supplies the missing August-case admission day. The memorial's broader recollections are not used to override the court's individual disposition. His existing identified portrait is retained.

operations.name: Alfred Fattig

expected.name: Alfred Fattig
expected.description: Alfred Fattig was an Oregon pacifist raised in the Church of the Brethren. After registering for the World War I draft, he wrote that he opposed war and then hid with his brother Charlie in the mountains of southwestern Oregon for three years rather than enter military service. He surrendered on July 26, 1920, pleaded guilty three days later, and served nine months in Multnomah County Jail. The Swarthmore College Peace Collection records him among imprisoned World War I conscientious objectors; his nephew Paul Fattig documented the brothers’ history in Madstone.

operations.name: Charles Savannah Fattig

expected.name: Charles Savannah Fattig
expected.description: Charles “Charlie” Savannah Fattig was an Oregon pacifist raised in the Church of the Brethren. He and his younger brother Alfred hid in the mountains of southwestern Oregon rather than comply with the World War I draft. Indicted for failing to appear for a physical examination, Charlie remained at large after Alfred surrendered in 1920. He surrendered the following year and served the same nine-month jail term. The Swarthmore College Peace Collection records his name as Charles Svannah Fattig; family historian Paul Fattig gives the middle name as Savannah.

operations.name: Leopold B. Galner

expected.name: Leopold B. Galner
expected.description: Leopold B. Galner was a Pennsylvania conscientious objector during World War I. He entered Camp Meade on September 21, 1917, declared his objection three days later, and was prosecuted for disobeying military orders. A court-martial sentenced him to fifteen years in prison, and he was held at Fort Leavenworth. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

operations.name: Oscar Ervin Hartman

expected.name: Oscar Ervin Hartman
expected.description: Oscar Ervin Hartman was a Virginia Mennonite conscientious objector. He refused induction in May 1918 and hid in the Virginia hills rather than report to Camp Lee. Hartman surrendered on June 1, 1920, was court-martialed, sentenced to three months of hard labor, and lost his citizenship. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

operations.name: David B. Hostetler

expected.name: David B. Hostetler
expected.description: David B. Hostetler was a Pennsylvania Mennonite conscientious objector. He did not report for induction at Camp Meade in April 1918, was arrested on April 30, and was court-martialed on June 18. He received a five-year prison sentence. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

expected.name: Emil W. Krieger
expected.description: Emil W. Krieger was a World War I conscientious objector sent to Fort Riley, Kansas. He refused to wear the uniform or perform military duties of any kind. A court-martial sentenced him to fifteen years in prison. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

operations.name: Chris E. Miller

expected.name: Chris E. Miller
expected.description: Chris E. Miller was a Kansas Mennonite conscientious objector assigned to Camp MacArthur, Texas, during World War I. He refused to cut fuel for a kitchen stove, drill, or wear the military uniform. He was court-martialed and sentenced to two years in prison. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

operations.name: J. Holmes Smith

expected.name: J. Holmes Smith
expected.description: J. Holmes Smith was a former Methodist missionary in India and a cofounder of the interracial Harlem Ashram. Police arrested him outside the British Embassy on February 22, 1943 while he picketed for the release of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru. Smith and Ralph Templin announced that they would conduct a hunger strike in jail.
